items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "genotype".
items.answer: The combination of alleles an organism has for a gene, e.g. Bb
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the combination of alleles an organism has for a gene, e.g. Bb. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: "Recessive alleles are weaker and eventually disappear from a population." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Recessive alleles can persist hidden in heterozygous carriers for many generations.
items.markingKey: Recessive alleles can persist hidden in heterozygous carriers for many generations. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between homozygous and heterozygous.
items.answer: Homozygous means two identical alleles (TT or tt); heterozygous means two different alleles (Tt).
items.markingKey: Homozygous means two identical alleles (TT or tt); heterozygous means two different alleles (Tt). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which ABO blood groups in transfusion shows codominance and recessive alleles.
items.answer: People with group O have genotype IᴼIᴼ; group AB people are IᴬIᴮ and show both antigens. Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant with each other and both dominant over Iᴼ, which explains the four blood groups.
items.markingKey: Context (People with group O have genotype IᴼIᴼ; group AB people are IᴬIᴮ and show both antigens.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant with each other and both dominant over Iᴼ, which explains the four blood groups. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to codominance and recessive alleles.

items.stem: With reference to ABO blood groups in transfusion, explain how it illustrates codominance and recessive alleles.
items.answer: People with group O have genotype IᴼIᴼ; group AB people are IᴬIᴮ and show both antigens. Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant with each other and both dominant over Iᴼ, which explains the four blood groups.
items.markingKey: Context (People with group O have genotype IᴼIᴼ; group AB people are IᴬIᴮ and show both antigens.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant with each other and both dominant over Iᴼ, which explains the four blood groups. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to codominance and recessive alleles.

items.stem: A guinea pig with black fur (B dominant to b, white) may be BB or Bb. Design a breeding test to find its genotype, predicting the offspring for each possibility with Punnett squares, and explain how many offspring you would need before you could be confident of the result.
items.answer: Cross with bb (white). If BB: all offspring Bb – black. If Bb: 1/2 black, 1/2 white. One white offspring proves Bb. If, e.g., 8 offspring are all black, the probability of this from Bb is (1/2)⁸ ≈ 0.4%, so BB is very likely; more offspring increase confidence.
items.markingKey: Cross with bb (white). If BB: all offspring Bb – black. If Bb: 1/2 black, 1/2 white. One white offspring proves Bb. If, e.g., 8 offspring are all black, the probability of this from Bb is (1/2)⁸ ≈ 0.4%, so BB is very likely; more offspring increase confidence.

items.stem: In sunflowers, yellow petals (Y) is dominant to red petals (y). Which statement describes an individual with genotype YY?
options: Homozygous dominant, with the phenotype red petals
Homozygous dominant, with the phenotype yellow petals
Homozygous recessive, with the phenotype red petals
Heterozygous, with the phenotype yellow petals
items.answer: Homozygous dominant, with the phenotype yellow petals
items.markingKey: B. Two identical dominant alleles.

items.stem: Noah writes: "A dominant allele is always the most common allele in a population." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Dominance describes expression in a heterozygote, not frequency; e.g. the allele for Huntington’s disease is dominant but rare.
items.markingKey: Dominance describes expression in a heterozygote, not frequency; e.g. the allele for Huntington’s disease is dominant but rare. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Kwame wants to find out whether the light intensity seedlings are grown in affects the proportion of albino (white) maize seedlings from a heterozygous cross. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does light intensity affect number of green and white seedlings?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (light intensity (lux, set by distance from a lamp)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (number of green and white seedlings counted after 10 days, expressed as a percentage) in a question form.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that genetic modification of crops to add useful dominant alleles (e.g. Bt maize, Golden Rice) should be encouraged.
items.answer: GM crops can bring large benefits when they are well regulated and accessible to small farmers.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: increases yields and reduces pesticide use (Bt crops); Golden Rice provides vitamin A where deficiency causes blindness. Arguments against: possible spread of genes to wild relatives; seed patents increase farmer dependence on companies; public distrust and labelling issues. Supported judgement: GM crops can bring large benefits when they are well regulated and accessible to small farmers. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: A cross between TT and tt plants gives what F1 offspring?
items.answer: All heterozygous and tall
items.markingKey: A. Every gamete from TT is T and every gamete from tt is t, so all offspring are Tt.

items.stem: "Two heterozygous parents already have three tall children, so the next child must be dwarf." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Each fertilisation is independent; the probability of a dwarf child is still 1/4.
items.markingKey: Each fertilisation is independent; the probability of a dwarf child is still 1/4. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why a 3 : 1 phenotype ratio suggests that both parents are heterozygous.
items.answer: Only Aa × Aa produces the genotypes AA, Aa, Aa, aa in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio, giving 3 dominant : 1 recessive phenotypes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Only Aa × Aa produces the genotypes AA, Aa, Aa, aa in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio, giving 3 dominant : 1 recessive phenotypes. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Lars modelled a monohybrid cross by drawing pairs of beads (one from each of two bags containing equal numbers of A and a beads) and calculated the ratio of dominant to recessive phenotypes for different numbers of draws.

Number of draws | Dominant : recessive ratio / x : 1: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
40 | 2.50 | 2.65 | 2.67
80 | 2.51 | 2.58 | 2.54
120 | 2.67 | 2.57 | 2.47
160 | 2.67 | 2.59 | 2.61
200 | 2.51 | 2.49 | 2.65

State the number of draws at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 120 ; range = 0.20 x : 1; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 120 ; 1 range = max − min = 2.67 − 2.47 = 0.20 x : 1; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: Diego plans to investigate whether drawing coloured beads from two bags (to model gametes from two heterozygous parents) gives a ratio closer to 3 : 1 as the number of draws increases. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: number of each colour in each bag (equal numbers); replacing beads after each draw; drawing without looking
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: number of each colour in each bag (equal numbers) – models a heterozygous parent producing 50% of each gamete; replacing beads after each draw – keeps the probability of each allele at 0.5; drawing without looking – keeps the selection random. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: Amara writes: "Two heterozygous parents already have three tall children, so the next child must be dwarf." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Each fertilisation is independent; the probability of a dwarf child is still 1/4.
items.markingKey: Each fertilisation is independent; the probability of a dwarf child is still 1/4. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Punnett squares are a reliable way for families to predict inherited disorders."
items.answer: Useful for single-gene conditions where the parents’ genotypes are known, but limited as a general prediction tool.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they give accurate probabilities for single-gene disorders such as cystic fibrosis; they help genetic counsellors explain risk. Arguments against: they give probabilities, not certainties, for each child; many conditions are polygenic or affected by environment; parents’ genotypes may be unknown without testing. Supported judgement: Useful for single-gene conditions where the parents’ genotypes are known, but limited as a general prediction tool.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate whether drawing coloured beads from two bags (to model gametes from two heterozygous parents) gives a ratio closer to 3 : 1 as the number of draws increases. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Put 50 red (A) and 50 white (a) beads in each of two bags; draw one bead from each bag without looking, record the pair, replace; do 10, 20, 50, 100 and 200 draws; count AA/Aa (dominant) and aa; calculate the ratio and percentage difference from 3 : 1; repeat each sample size three times.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (pick up any spilled beads to avoid slipping). Model: Put 50 red (A) and 50 white (a) beads in each of two bags; draw one bead from each bag without looking, record the pair, replace; do 10, 20, 50, 100 and 200 draws; count AA/Aa (dominant) and aa; calculate the ratio and percentage difference from 3 : 1; repeat each sample size three times.

items.stem: Explain why the ratios predicted by a Punnett square are rarely obtained exactly in real crosses.
items.answer: Each fertilisation is a random event, so the ratios are probabilities; with small numbers of offspring chance variation means the observed ratio differs from the expected ratio – larger samples come closer.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each fertilisation is a random event, so the ratios are probabilities; with small numbers of offspring chance variation means the observed ratio differs from the expected ratio – larger samples come closer. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that in a Punnett square the alleles of one parent are written along both sides. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: One parent’s gametes go along the top and the other parent’s gametes down the side.
items.markingKey: One parent’s gametes go along the top and the other parent’s gametes down the side. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In cats, the allele for short hair (S) is dominant to the allele for long hair (s). An individual with genotype SS is crossed with one with genotype ss. Use a Punnett square to give the expected genotype ratio and phenotype ratio of the offspring.
items.answer: Genotypes all Ss; phenotypes all short hair
items.markingKey: 1 correct gametes; 1 Punnett square (Gametes S, S × s, s; offspring Ss, Ss, Ss, Ss); 1 genotype ratio all Ss; 1 phenotype ratio all short hair.

items.stem:
Lukas is investigating whether drawing coloured beads from two bags (to model gametes from two heterozygous parents) gives a ratio closer to 3 : 1 as the number of draws increases.
(a) State the independent variable. [1]
(b) State the dependent variable and how it will be measured. [1]
(c) Identify two control variables and explain why each must be kept constant. [2]
(d) Formulate a testable hypothesis and explain it using scientific reasoning. [2]
items.answer: (a) number of pairs of beads drawn (10, 20, 50, 100, 200). (b) ratio of “dominant” to “recessive” phenotypes – counted from the bead pairs and calculated as x : 1. (c) number of each colour in each bag (equal numbers) – models a heterozygous parent producing 50% of each gamete; drawing without looking – keeps the selection random. (d) If more pairs are drawn, then the ratio will get closer to 3 : 1, because each draw is a random event and the effect of chance variation decreases with larger samples.
items.markingKey: (a) 1: number of pairs of beads drawn (10, 20, 50, 100, 200). (b) 1: ratio of “dominant” to “recessive” phenotypes – counted from the bead pairs and calculated as x : 1 (must include how/units). (c) 1 each, variable + reason: any two of number of each colour in each bag (equal numbers) (models a heterozygous parent producing 50% of each gamete); replacing beads after each draw (keeps the probability of each allele at 0.5); drawing without looking (keeps the selection random). (d) 1 for a testable if/then prediction linking IV and DV, 1 for correct scientific reasoning: If more pairs are drawn, then the ratio will get closer to 3 : 1, because each draw is a random event and the effect of chance variation decreases with larger samples.

items.stem: Which parent determines the sex of a human baby?
options: The mother, because eggs carry X or Y
The father, because sperm carry either an X or a Y chromosome
items.answer: The father, because sperm carry either an X or a Y chromosome
items.markingKey: D. All eggs carry X; half of sperm carry X and half carry Y.

items.stem: Explain why a colour-blind man cannot pass colour blindness to his son.
items.answer: A father passes his Y chromosome to his sons, not his X; the colour-blindness allele is on the X chromosome, so sons inherit the X from their mother.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A father passes his Y chromosome to his sons, not his X; the colour-blindness allele is on the X chromosome, so sons inherit the X from their mother. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Haemophilia only affects males because the allele is on the Y chromosome." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The allele is on the X chromosome; females can be affected (XʰXʰ) but it is rare.
items.markingKey: The allele is on the X chromosome; females can be affected (XʰXʰ) but it is rare. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that boys get their X chromosome from their father. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Boys get their Y from their father and their X from their mother.
items.markingKey: Boys get their Y from their father and their X from their mother. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: For Duchenne muscular dystrophy (recessive allele Xd), parents with genotypes XDXD and XDY are expecting a son. What is the probability that he will be affected?
items.markingKey: 1 a son receives Y from the father and one X from the mother (XD or XD); 1 probability 0/2 = 0%.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Parents should be allowed to choose the sex of their baby using IVF and embryo testing."
items.answer: Many countries allow selection only to avoid serious sex-linked disease, not for social reasons; this balances health benefits with social risks.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: can avoid serious sex-linked disorders such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy; reproductive freedom. Arguments against: could unbalance sex ratios in societies with a son preference; treats children as products; slippery slope to designer babies; IVF is expensive and has health risks. Supported judgement: Many countries allow selection only to avoid serious sex-linked disease, not for social reasons; this balances health benefits with social risks.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "sex-linked characteristic".
items.answer: A characteristic controlled by a gene carried on a sex chromosome, usually the X chromosome
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a characteristic controlled by a gene carried on a sex chromosome, usually the X chromosome. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Zara writes: "After three girls, a couple is more likely to have a boy next time." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Each pregnancy is independent; the probability of a boy is still about 0.5.
items.markingKey: Each pregnancy is independent; the probability of a boy is still about 0.5. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe haemophilia in Queen Victoria’s descendants and explain what it reveals about X-linked recessive inheritance.
items.answer: Queen Victoria was a carrier; her son Leopold had haemophilia and two daughters were carriers who passed it into the Spanish and Russian royal families. Carrier females passed Xʰ to about half their sons (affected) and half their daughters (carriers), while no male in the line passed it to a son.
items.markingKey: Context (Queen Victoria was a carrier; her son Leopold had haemophilia and two daughters were carriers who passed it into the Spanish and Russian royal families.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Carrier females passed Xʰ to about half their sons (affected) and half their daughters (carriers), while no male in the line passed it to a son. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to X-linked recessive inheritance.

items.stem: A woman whose father had haemophilia marries a man without haemophilia. (a) Deduce the woman’s genotype and explain how you know. (b) Draw a Punnett square for their children. (c) State the probability that a son will have haemophilia and that a daughter will be a carrier.
items.answer: (a) XᴴXʰ – her father gave her his only X, which carried Xʰ, but she is unaffected. (b) XᴴXʰ × XᴴY → XᴴXᴴ, XᴴY, XʰXᴴ, XʰY. (c) son affected 1/2; daughter carrier 1/2.
items.markingKey: (a) XᴴXʰ – her father gave her his only X, which carried Xʰ, but she is unaffected. (b) XᴴXʰ × XᴴY → XᴴXᴴ, XᴴY, XʰXᴴ, XʰY. (c) son affected 1/2; daughter carrier 1/2.

items.stem: In a pedigree chart, what does a shaded square usually represent?
items.answer: An affected male
items.markingKey: D. Squares are males, circles are females; shading shows the trait.

items.stem: Distinguish between an autosomal recessive disorder and an autosomal dominant disorder.
items.answer: A recessive disorder appears only in homozygous recessive people and can skip generations through carriers; a dominant disorder appears with one allele and every affected person has an affected parent.
items.markingKey: A recessive disorder appears only in homozygous recessive people and can skip generations through carriers; a dominant disorder appears with one allele and every affected person has an affected parent. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why Huntington’s disease can be passed on even though it is caused by a dominant allele.
items.answer: Symptoms usually appear at 35-45 years, often after the person has had children, so the allele is passed on before the person knows they have it.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Symptoms usually appear at 35-45 years, often after the person has had children, so the allele is passed on before the person knows they have it. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Kenji has phenylketonuria (PKU) (a recessive disorder). Tariq is a carrier. What is the probability that their child will have phenylketonuria (PKU)?
items.markingKey: 1 genotypes pp × Pp; 1 offspring Pp, Pp, pp, pp; 1 probability 1/2.

items.stem: "Cystic fibrosis is caused by bacteria in the lungs, so it can be caught." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: CF is an inherited disorder caused by a recessive allele; lung infections are a consequence of the thick mucus, not the cause.
items.markingKey: CF is an inherited disorder caused by a recessive allele; lung infections are a consequence of the thick mucus, not the cause. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that embryos created by IVF should be screened so that only those without inherited disorders are implanted.
items.answer: Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis for serious disorders is accepted in many countries under regulation; selection for other traits is not.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: prevents suffering from serious disorders; carrier couples can have healthy children. Arguments against: destroys embryos, which some consider wrong; could lead to selection for non-medical traits; expensive and not available to all. Supported judgement: Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis for serious disorders is accepted in many countries under regulation; selection for other traits is not.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Testing people or embryos for alleles that cause inherited disorders"?
items.answer: genetic screening
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of genetic screening.

items.stem: A student claims that if one parent has a dominant disorder, all the children will have it. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: If that parent is heterozygous, each child has a 50% chance.
items.markingKey: If that parent is heterozygous, each child has a 50% chance. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
A newborn screening programme in Nia’s region recorded the number of babies diagnosed with cystic fibrosis per 100 000 births in five years after screening began.

Year after screening began | Diagnoses / per 100 000 births: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 39 | 38 | 38
2 | 41 | 39 | 39
3 | 39 | 38 | 41
4 | 39 | 39 | 41
5 | 41 | 40 | 41

Calculate the mean diagnoses when the year after screening began was 3 .
items.answer: 39.3 per 100 000 births
items.markingKey: M1 (39 + 38 + 41) ÷ 3; A1 39.3 per 100 000 births (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

Generation I: an unaffected man (1) and an unaffected woman (2). Generation II: their children – an affected daughter (3), an unaffected son (4) and an unaffected daughter (5). The affected daughter has cystic fibrosis.
— Pedigree description

Deduce the genotypes of individuals 1, 2 and 3 (F = normal, f = cystic fibrosis) and state the probability that individual 5 is a carrier.
items.answer: 1 and 2 must be Ff (unaffected parents of an ff child); 3 is ff; 5 is FF or Ff, unaffected, so the probability she is a carrier is 2/3.
items.markingKey: 1 and 2 must be Ff (unaffected parents of an ff child); 3 is ff; 5 is FF or Ff, unaffected, so the probability she is a carrier is 2/3. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "genetic variation"?
options: An autosomal dominant disorder causing progressive breakdown of nerve cells in the brain, usually from middle age
Differences caused by conditions such as diet, climate or lifestyle
Differences caused by the different alleles individuals inherit
Differences in characteristics between individuals of the same species
items.answer: Differences caused by the different alleles individuals inherit
items.markingKey: C. "genetic variation" is differences caused by the different alleles individuals inherit.

items.stem: Briefly explain why height shows continuous variation.
items.answer: Height is controlled by many genes (polygenic), each adding a small amount, and by environmental factors such as diet, so it can take any value within a range and forms a normal distribution.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Height is controlled by many genes (polygenic), each adding a small amount, and by environmental factors such as diet, so it can take any value within a range and forms a normal distribution. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Hana measured the length of ivy leaves (30 leaves per site) at sites with different light intensities.

Light intensity / klux | Mean leaf length / mm: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
2 | 74.3 | 72.4 | 73.6
5 | 63.5 | 61.3 | 61.6
10 | 56.1 | 55.6 | 56.1
20 | 50.9 | 49.3 | 53.2
40 | 45.8 | 46.2 | 46.7

Calculate the mean mean leaf length when the light intensity was 5 klux.
items.markingKey: M1 (63.5 + 61.3 + 61.6) ÷ 3; A1 62.13 mm (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Nia wants to find out whether the leaves of ivy growing in shade are larger than the leaves of ivy growing in full sunlight. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does light exposure affect leaf surface area?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (light exposure (shade or full sun, measured with a light meter in lux)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (leaf surface area – traced on 1 cm² grid paper and squares counted) in a question form.

items.stem: A class measured the heights of 30 students and the blood groups of the same students. Explain which type of graph should be used for each data set, describe the expected shape of the height graph, and explain the causes of the variation in each characteristic.
items.answer: Height: continuous – histogram with grouped classes; roughly normal (bell-shaped) distribution; caused by many genes plus environment (diet, health). Blood group: discontinuous – bar chart with gaps; four categories; caused by a single gene with three alleles, not affected by the environment.
items.markingKey: Height: continuous – histogram with grouped classes; roughly normal (bell-shaped) distribution; caused by many genes plus environment (diet, health). Blood group: discontinuous – bar chart with gaps; four categories; caused by a single gene with three alleles, not affected by the environment.

items.stem: Briefly explain why genetically identical plants grown from cuttings can still differ in height.
items.answer: They have the same alleles, so differences must be environmental – e.g. light, water, minerals and temperature.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They have the same alleles, so differences must be environmental – e.g. light, water, minerals and temperature. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Elena writes: "Bar charts with gaps are the best way to show the heights of a class." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Height is continuous; group it into classes and draw a histogram with no gaps.
items.markingKey: Height is continuous; group it into classes and draw a histogram with no gaps. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Leila investigated whether the leaves of ivy growing in shade are larger than the leaves of ivy growing in full sunlight. The method had this weakness: the largest leaves were chosen by eye at each site. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: select leaves randomly (e.g. random numbers to choose stems) so the sample represents the whole population
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: select leaves randomly (e.g. random numbers to choose stems) so the sample represents the whole population

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "F1 generation".
items.answer: The first generation of offspring from a cross between two parents
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the first generation of offspring from a cross between two parents. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A pea plant has the genotype Tt, where T (tall) is dominant. What is its phenotype?
items.answer: Tall
items.markingKey: C. One dominant allele is enough for the tall phenotype.

items.stem: What is the probability that a human baby will be a boy?
items.markingKey: 0.5. XX × XY gives XX, XX, XY, XY.

items.stem: Zara writes: "A disorder that skips a generation in a pedigree must be dominant." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Skipping generations is typical of recessive alleles hidden in carriers.
items.markingKey: Skipping generations is typical of recessive alleles hidden in carriers. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that a bodybuilder’s large muscles will be inherited by her children. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Muscle size from training is environmental variation, which is not passed on in the DNA.
items.markingKey: Muscle size from training is environmental variation, which is not passed on in the DNA. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Alessia writes: "In a Punnett square the alleles of one parent are written along both sides." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: One parent’s gametes go along the top and the other parent’s gametes down the side.
items.markingKey: One parent’s gametes go along the top and the other parent’s gametes down the side. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why an organism with the dominant phenotype may have one of two genotypes.
items.answer: A dominant allele is expressed with one copy, so both the homozygous (BB) and the heterozygous (Bb) genotype show the same phenotype.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A dominant allele is expressed with one copy, so both the homozygous (BB) and the heterozygous (Bb) genotype show the same phenotype. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Isabel writes: "Boys get their X chromosome from their father." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Boys get their Y from their father and their X from their mother.
items.markingKey: Boys get their Y from their father and their X from their mother. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "A disorder that skips a generation in a pedigree must be dominant." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Skipping generations is typical of recessive alleles hidden in carriers.
items.markingKey: Skipping generations is typical of recessive alleles hidden in carriers. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Diego measured the lengths of holly leaves (mm): 73, 61, 69, 54, 55, 65, 47, 46. Calculate the mean and the range, and state the type of variation shown.
items.answer: mean = 58.8 mm; range = 27 mm; continuous variation
items.markingKey: M1 sum ÷ 8; A1 mean 58.8 mm; A1 range 73 − 46 = 27 mm; 1 continuous (any value in a range).

items.stem: A student claims that if two Tt plants have four offspring, exactly three will be tall and one will be dwarf. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The 3 : 1 ratio is a probability for each offspring (75% tall); four offspring could be any combination by chance.
items.markingKey: The 3 : 1 ratio is a probability for each offspring (75% tall); four offspring could be any combination by chance. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that a dominant allele is always the most common allele in a population. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Dominance describes expression in a heterozygote, not frequency; e.g. the allele for Huntington’s disease is dominant but rare.
items.markingKey: Dominance describes expression in a heterozygote, not frequency; e.g. the allele for Huntington’s disease is dominant but rare. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which haemophilia in Queen Victoria’s descendants shows X-linked recessive inheritance.
items.answer: Queen Victoria was a carrier; her son Leopold had haemophilia and two daughters were carriers who passed it into the Spanish and Russian royal families. Carrier females passed Xʰ to about half their sons (affected) and half their daughters (carriers), while no male in the line passed it to a son.
items.markingKey: Context (Queen Victoria was a carrier; her son Leopold had haemophilia and two daughters were carriers who passed it into the Spanish and Russian royal families.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Carrier females passed Xʰ to about half their sons (affected) and half their daughters (carriers), while no male in the line passed it to a son. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to X-linked recessive inheritance.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the number of generations included in a family pedigree affects how confidently a disorder can be identified as dominant or recessive (using pedigree data from a genetic counselling database), state the dependent variable and describe how Tomás should measure it.
items.answer: percentage of pedigrees correctly classified as dominant or recessive by a panel of students
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: percentage of pedigrees correctly classified as dominant or recessive by a panel of students.

items.stem: Briefly describe hydrangeas in different gardens and explain what it reveals about environmental variation.
items.answer: The same variety has blue flowers in acidic soil and pink flowers in alkaline soil. The genotype is the same, but soil pH changes the availability of aluminium ions and therefore the flower colour.
items.markingKey: Context (The same variety has blue flowers in acidic soil and pink flowers in alkaline soil.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The genotype is the same, but soil pH changes the availability of aluminium ions and therefore the flower colour. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to environmental variation.

items.stem: In tomato plants, the allele for red fruit (R) is dominant to the allele for yellow fruit (r). An individual with genotype RR is crossed with one with genotype rr. Use a Punnett square to give the expected genotype ratio and phenotype ratio of the offspring.
items.answer: Genotypes all Rr; phenotypes all red fruit
items.markingKey: 1 correct gametes; 1 Punnett square (Gametes R, R × r, r; offspring Rr, Rr, Rr, Rr); 1 genotype ratio all Rr; 1 phenotype ratio all red fruit.

items.stem: Chloé investigated whether the light intensity seedlings are grown in affects the proportion of albino (white) maize seedlings from a heterozygous cross. The method had this weakness: only 12 seeds were sown in each tray. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: sow at least 100 seeds per tray: genetic ratios are probabilities, so small samples can differ greatly from 3 : 1 by chance
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: sow at least 100 seeds per tray: genetic ratios are probabilities, so small samples can differ greatly from 3 : 1 by chance

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that gene therapy for haemophilia, costing over US$2 million per patient, should be funded by public health systems.
items.answer: It can be cost-effective over a lifetime, but funding decisions must weigh long-term evidence and fairness of access.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: a single treatment can replace a lifetime of expensive clotting-factor injections; greatly improves quality of life. Arguments against: very high upfront cost limits other healthcare spending; long-term safety and durability not yet known; unequal access between rich and poor countries. Supported judgement: It can be cost-effective over a lifetime, but funding decisions must weigh long-term evidence and fairness of access. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Alessia plans an investigation into how the number of generations included in a family pedigree affects how confidently a disorder can be identified as dominant or recessive (using pedigree data from a genetic counselling database). Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (number of generations included (2, 3, 4, 5)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: "Most human characteristics are determined by genes rather than the environment." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Most characteristics result from an interaction of genes and environment; only a few are purely genetic.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: blood group, eye colour and many disorders are genetic; twin studies show high heritability for height. Arguments against: most features are polygenic and influenced by environment (body mass, skin colour, intelligence); gene expression is affected by environment. Supported judgement: Most characteristics result from an interaction of genes and environment; only a few are purely genetic. Markbands (15 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Crossing an individual of unknown genotype with a homozygous recessive individual to reveal its genotype"?
items.answer: test cross
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of test cross.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "dominant allele"?
options: An allele that is expressed in the phenotype even if only one copy is present (written with a capital letter)
Differences caused by the different alleles individuals inherit
A grid used to show all possible combinations of parental gametes and predict the probability of offspring genotypes
A condition caused by a faulty allele that is passed from parents to offspring
items.answer: An allele that is expressed in the phenotype even if only one copy is present (written with a capital letter)
items.markingKey: A. "dominant allele" is an allele that is expressed in the phenotype even if only one copy is present (written with a capital letter).

items.stem: Define the term "sex chromosomes".
items.answer: The pair of chromosomes that determines sex: XX in human females and XY in human males
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the pair of chromosomes that determines sex: XX in human females and XY in human males. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an autosomal dominant disorder and an autosomal recessive disorder.
items.answer: A recessive disorder appears only in homozygous recessive people and can skip generations through carriers; a dominant disorder appears with one allele and every affected person has an affected parent.
items.markingKey: A recessive disorder appears only in homozygous recessive people and can skip generations through carriers; a dominant disorder appears with one allele and every affected person has an affected parent. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "A bodybuilder’s large muscles will be inherited by her children." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Muscle size from training is environmental variation, which is not passed on in the DNA.
items.markingKey: Muscle size from training is environmental variation, which is not passed on in the DNA. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why each gamete carries only one allele of each gene.
items.answer: In meiosis homologous chromosomes separate, so each haploid gamete receives one chromosome of each pair and therefore one allele of each gene.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: In meiosis homologous chromosomes separate, so each haploid gamete receives one chromosome of each pair and therefore one allele of each gene. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain what a test cross is and why it is used.
items.answer: An organism with the dominant phenotype is crossed with a homozygous recessive one; if any offspring show the recessive phenotype the unknown parent must be heterozygous, otherwise it is probably homozygous dominant.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: An organism with the dominant phenotype is crossed with a homozygous recessive one; if any offspring show the recessive phenotype the unknown parent must be heterozygous, otherwise it is probably homozygous dominant. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between an autosome and a sex chromosome.
items.answer: Sex chromosomes (X and Y) determine sex and differ between males and females; autosomes are the other 22 pairs, the same in both sexes.
items.markingKey: Sex chromosomes (X and Y) determine sex and differ between males and females; autosomes are the other 22 pairs, the same in both sexes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why marriages between close relatives increase the chance of children with recessive disorders.
items.answer: Relatives share many alleles from common ancestors, so both are more likely to carry the same rare recessive allele, increasing the chance of a homozygous recessive child.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Relatives share many alleles from common ancestors, so both are more likely to carry the same rare recessive allele, increasing the chance of a homozygous recessive child. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to hydrangeas in different gardens, explain how it illustrates environmental variation.
items.answer: The same variety has blue flowers in acidic soil and pink flowers in alkaline soil. The genotype is the same, but soil pH changes the availability of aluminium ions and therefore the flower colour.
items.markingKey: Context (The same variety has blue flowers in acidic soil and pink flowers in alkaline soil.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The genotype is the same, but soil pH changes the availability of aluminium ions and therefore the flower colour. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to environmental variation.

items.stem: A student claims that two heterozygous parents already have three tall children, so the next child must be dwarf. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Each fertilisation is independent; the probability of a dwarf child is still 1/4.
items.markingKey: Each fertilisation is independent; the probability of a dwarf child is still 1/4. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Gregor Mendel’s pea-plant experiments in Brno (1856-1863) as an example, explain dominant and recessive alleles.
items.answer: Crossing true-breeding tall and dwarf plants gave all-tall offspring; self-crossing these gave a 3 : 1 ratio of tall to dwarf. The dwarf trait disappeared in the first generation and reappeared in the second, showing the recessive allele was present but hidden in heterozygotes.
items.markingKey: Context (Crossing true-breeding tall and dwarf plants gave all-tall offspring; self-crossing these gave a 3 : 1 ratio of tall to dwarf.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The dwarf trait disappeared in the first generation and reappeared in the second, showing the recessive allele was present but hidden in heterozygotes. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to dominant and recessive alleles.

items.stem: "After three girls, a couple is more likely to have a boy next time." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Each pregnancy is independent; the probability of a boy is still about 0.5.
items.markingKey: Each pregnancy is independent; the probability of a boy is still about 0.5. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that a disorder that skips a generation in a pedigree must be dominant. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Skipping generations is typical of recessive alleles hidden in carriers.
items.markingKey: Skipping generations is typical of recessive alleles hidden in carriers. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that bar charts with gaps are the best way to show the heights of a class. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Height is continuous; group it into classes and draw a histogram with no gaps.
items.markingKey: Height is continuous; group it into classes and draw a histogram with no gaps. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "In a Punnett square the alleles of one parent are written along both sides." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: One parent’s gametes go along the top and the other parent’s gametes down the side.
items.markingKey: One parent’s gametes go along the top and the other parent’s gametes down the side. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Knowing a person’s genotype tells you everything about their phenotype."
items.answer: Genotype is important but phenotype usually results from genotype interacting with the environment, so the claim is only true for a few single-gene characteristics.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: some single-gene traits (e.g. ABO blood group, cystic fibrosis) are determined by genotype; genotype sets the possible range of features. Arguments against: many traits are polygenic and influenced by environment (height, skin colour, intelligence); gene expression can be switched on or off by environmental factors. Supported judgement: Genotype is important but phenotype usually results from genotype interacting with the environment, so the claim is only true for a few single-gene characteristics.

items.stem: Arjun investigated how the incubation temperature of eggs affects the percentage of female hatchlings in a species of turtle (using published data from a conservation project). The method had this weakness: eggs at different temperatures came from different beaches and species. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: use eggs from the same species and population, randomly allocated to each temperature
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: use eggs from the same species and population, randomly allocated to each temperature

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that all newborn babies should be screened for inherited disorders.
items.answer: Screening for treatable disorders is widely justified; screening for untreatable ones raises more ethical questions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: early treatment improves outcomes (e.g. diet for PKU, physiotherapy for CF); relatively cheap heel-prick test; parents learn their carrier status for future pregnancies. Arguments against: false positives cause anxiety; some disorders have no treatment; genetic data privacy; cost to health services. Supported judgement: Screening for treatable disorders is widely justified; screening for untreatable ones raises more ethical questions. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into whether the leaves of ivy growing in shade are larger than the leaves of ivy growing in full sunlight. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): wear gloves – ivy sap can irritate skin; take care near walls and roads. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. wear gloves – ivy sap can irritate skin; take care near walls and roads); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.
